The flight and expulsion of about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs from their homes during the 1947 to 1949 war in Palestine, the war in which the state of Israel was founded. Nakba is Arabic for "catastrophe". More than half the Arab population of Palestine lost their homes, and most were never allowed to return.

The war began as a civil war after the United Nations voted in November 1947 to split Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state. It became a war between states when Israel declared independence in May 1948 and neighbouring Arab armies invaded.

What happened:

  • Hundreds of Arab villages were emptied, and most were later destroyed or resettled.
  • Some people fled the fighting or fear of massacre, especially after the killings at Deir Yassin in April 1948. Others were driven out, as at Lydda and Ramle in July 1948.
  • Israel decided early not to let refugees return, and took over their land and property by law.

The refugees ended up in the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. The United Nations set up UNRWA in 1949 to support them, and their descendants now number in the millions. Why they left was argued for decades; research in Israeli archives from the 1980s showed that expulsion, attacks and fear all played a part.

Palestinians mark 15 May as Nakba Day, and many also use the word for their continuing displacement since. In the same years many Jews left or were pushed out of Arab countries, in the Jewish exodus from Arab lands, and most went to Israel.
